liturgical_day: Wednesday of the Eighteenth Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: Great is your faith
theme: The Canaanite woman receives silence and apparent refusal without surrendering her trust; humble persistence discovers that even the smallest gift from Christ’s table is more than enough.
introduction: Jesus withdraws beyond Israel’s familiar borders, and a Canaanite woman comes out to meet him with her daughter’s misery as her own. She names him Lord and Son of David, but he first answers with silence. The disciples hear only a troubling cry behind them; the woman hears no permission to abandon hope. Even when Jesus states the order of his mission and speaks of the children’s bread, she does not deny Israel’s place or demand a right. She worships, asks for help, and finds within his image of the household a place for mercy: crumbs still fall from the masters’ table. Her reply holds together humility and astonishing confidence. Christ brings her faith into the open, praises it as great, and heals her daughter by his word. The passage teaches prayer that remains truthful, reverent, and bold when grace seems delayed.
hero_alt: The Canaanite woman kneels in persevering prayer before Christ near the coast of Tyre and Sidon as disciples watch, rendered in Byzantine mosaic, stained glass, gold leaf, and luminous geometry
closing_title: Remain at the table of mercy
closing: The woman’s greatness does not lie in winning an argument with Jesus. She receives the truth about Israel’s promised place, refuses resentment, and entrusts herself more completely to the Lord whose mercy she seeks. Her prayer becomes shorter as the trial deepens: from a full account of her daughter’s suffering to the bare cry, “Lord, help me,” and finally to a humble assent that discovers abundance in a crumb. The Catena’s Fathers see Christ’s delay not as indifference but as a revelation of faith already at work within her. What the disciples cannot secure by urging dismissal, persevering prayer receives through direct dependence on Christ. The encounter also opens toward the nations: the outsider recognizes Israel’s Messiah and is welcomed through faith. Christian persistence is therefore neither entitlement nor denial of pain. It stays near, accepts correction, and continues asking because the smallest gift from the Lord’s table carries the power of the Lord himself.

verses.text: And Jesus left there and withdrew into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon.
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Christ leaves the cavilling leaders and approaches Gentile territory. The change of place prepares a healing that reveals mercy already reaching beyond Israel’s borders.
verses.commentary: Jerome contrasts Christ’s departure from the scribes and Pharisees with his movement toward Tyre and Sidon, where healing will appear among Gentiles. Remigius identifies the cities as Canaanite territory and sees the journey directed toward the woman’s afflicted daughter. The movement is therefore more than geography: Jesus leaves hardened dispute and enters a boundary place where unexpected faith will be disclosed. Yet he does not abandon the order of salvation or turn his mission into spectacle. The scene quietly prepares the meeting in which a woman from outside Israel will recognize Israel’s Messiah and cling to his mercy.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, with Remigius, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: And behold, a woman of Canaan came out from those coasts and cried aloud to him, saying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously troubled by the devil.”
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: The woman leaves her own territory and asks only for mercy. Her daughter’s torment has become her own wound, and she brings it directly to the Lord.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom emphasizes that the Evangelist names her a Canaanite to display what Christ’s presence has awakened: one from a people long separated from Israel now comes seeking Israel’s Messiah. She does not bargain or claim merit; she cries for mercy. The Catena’s Gloss notes the fullness of her confession: “Lord” acknowledges divine authority, while “Son of David” recognizes the promised human lineage. She says, “Have mercy on me,” because a mother bears her daughter’s affliction within herself. By naming both the severity and source of the torment, she lays the whole wound before the true Physician.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, Homily 52 on Matthew, with the Gloss, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away, for she is crying after us.”
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Christ’s silence draws the woman’s perseverance into view. The disciples are moved by her cry, but she must continue beyond their limited response toward the Lord himself.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom sets the woman’s wise confidence beside a fresh trial: after she has rejected every lesser remedy and run to the Lord, the Lover of mankind answers nothing. The silence is not the final word. It creates room for the steadfastness of her prayer to become visible. The disciples feel her affliction, though they do not yet dare to ask plainly for the healing; they urge that she be sent away because she continues crying after them. Her need cannot be resolved by their discomfort or compassion alone. She remains before Christ until the purpose hidden within the delay is revealed.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, Homily 52 on Matthew, with St Jerome, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: He answered and said, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Jesus states the promised order of his earthly mission: Israel first. The woman’s hope must pass through this truth rather than treating covenant history as though it did not matter.
verses.commentary: Jerome explains that Christ was sent first to Israel, so that the Gospel’s later passage to the Gentiles would follow Israel’s refusal rather than disregard God’s promises. Remigius likewise distinguishes Christ’s bodily ministry among the Jewish people from the wider salvation his word would accomplish. The saying therefore establishes an order in the divine mission; it does not declare that mercy can never reach this woman. Her faith will not grow by denying Israel’s place. It must recognize the Son of David within that history and continue trusting that his goodness is not exhausted by the priority he has just named.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, with Remigius, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: But she came and adored him, saying, “Lord, help me.”
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: Denied an easy answer, the woman draws nearer and adores. Her prayer loses every ornament until only trust remains: “Lord, help me.”
verses.commentary: Jerome traces the deepening confession in the woman’s approach. She first calls Jesus Son of David, then Lord, and now comes to adore him as God. Chrysostom observes that when appeal through the Apostles seems powerless, she advances with commendable boldness instead of withdrawing. Her words also become strikingly simple. She does not tell Christ to ask another or pray to God on her behalf; she says directly, “Lord, help me.” The brevity is not emptiness but concentrated faith. She places neither an argument nor a claim between herself and Christ, only worship and an urgent dependence upon his own power.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, with St John Chrysostom, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: He answered and said, “It is not good to take the children’s bread and cast it to the dogs.”
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: The image makes the trial sharper: Israel is named as the children who receive the bread first. Yet the household image will also give faith a way to confess both order and overflowing mercy.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom notes that the answer strengthens the apparent refusal: Israel is no longer described only as sheep, but as children, while the Gentiles are placed outside that privilege. The Catena’s Gloss identifies the bread with the Gospel, Christ’s miracles, and the gifts belonging to salvation. The saying preserves the children’s rightful priority and refuses to make covenant history meaningless. At the same time, Christ gives the woman an image rather than closing the encounter. She will answer from within that very household, neither taking the children’s place nor imagining that the master’s table is too poor for mercy to overflow.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, Homily 52 on Matthew, with the Gloss, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: But she said, “Yes, Lord; for the little dogs also eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”
verses.author: St Jerome
verses.insight: She answers without contradiction or resentment. Humility accepts the place named, while faith sees that a crumb from this Master bears inexhaustible goodness.
verses.commentary: Jerome marvels at three virtues joined in her reply: faith that trusts Christ can heal, patience that persists after repeated delay, and humility that accepts the lowly image without revolt. She does not demand the children’s whole loaf or seize their seat. Yet neither does she leave the table of her Lord. Chrysostom stresses her prudence: she assents to Christ’s words, calls the children her masters, and discovers within the comparison itself the ground of her appeal. Crumbs do fall. Her humility is therefore not despair or self-erasure; it is the freedom to rely entirely on the abundance of another’s table.
verses.source_label: St Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, with St John Chrysostom, as collected in the Catena Aurea

verses.text: Then Jesus answered and said to her, “O woman, great is your faith. Let it be done to you as you will.” And her daughter was cured from that hour.
verses.author: St John Chrysostom
verses.insight: Christ publicly names the greatness his delay has uncovered. The mother’s persevering faith receives an immediate healing accomplished by the authority of his word.
verses.commentary: Chrysostom says Christ delayed because he knew the excellence of the woman’s answer and would not let such faith remain hidden. His praise confirms that her words were not flattery but the expression of a sincere and abundant trust. “Let it be done” also displays the creative authority of Christ’s word: as creation obeyed God’s command, the distant daughter is healed in that hour. The woman’s own earnest prayer obtains what the disciples’ intervention did not. The Father therefore urges believers not to surrender the personal work of prayer, even while the Church also prays for them. Persevering faith remains active before Christ.
verses.source_label: St John Chrysostom, Homily 52 on Matthew, as collected in the Catena Aurea
